name: South Port New Zealand Limited
company_overview: South Port New Zealand owns and operates the Port of Bluff, the southernmost commercial deepwater port in New Zealand and the sole seaport serving the Southland region. It handles bulk cargo (fertiliser, stock feed, cement, forestry products, alumina), containers, and marine/wharf services for the New Zealand Aluminium Smelter (NZAS) at nearby Tiwai Point, alongside warehousing and property leasing. The company is majority-owned (~66%) by Environment Southland, the regional council, with the remaining free float split between retail and institutional NZ investors.

business_model.summary: South Port earns wharfage, cargo handling, storage/warehousing, marine (towage, pilotage, stevedoring) and property/lease revenue from a diversified but geographically concentrated cargo base. Revenue is largely volume-linked (tonnes handled, TEU, vessel calls) rather than contracted/recurring in the SaaS sense, though a portion of Tiwai wharf income is understood to be fixed/take-or-pay regardless of tonnage, providing some downside cushion from its largest single customer. FY26 operating revenue was NZ$71.8-71.9m, up ~13.5-14% on FY25's $63.3m, with EBITDA margin of ~41.6-42%, roughly 100bps above the NZ port-sector average of ~38% (FY25) but below SPN's own 10-year peak of ~44%.

revenue_streams.name: Bulk cargo (Bluff Wharves) - fertiliser, stock feed, cement, forestry, acid, fuel
revenue_streams.basis: 59% of FY26 total trade volume per FY26 investor presentation; bulk volumes +9.7% (company release) / +7.3% (presentation slide) to ~3.3m tonnes

revenue_streams.name: Tiwai Wharf - NZAS aluminium smelter (alumina, petroleum coke/pitch imports; aluminium exports)
revenue_streams.basis: 24% of FY26 total trade volume; volumes +16.1% to 942k tonnes, still below pre-2025 historical levels per management

revenue_streams.name: Containers (TEU) - dairy, meat, aluminium products, general export/import
revenue_streams.basis: 17% of FY26 total trade volume; record 62,000 TEU, +18.5% YoY, supported by new MSC Eagle Service and Trans-Tasman Southern Loop

revenue_streams.name: Other - warehousing, cruise ships, other marine revenue
revenue_streams.basis: described as ~1% up on FY25, no precise percent of revenue disclosed

business_model.customer_type: B2B - concentrated regional exporters/importers (NZAS/Rio Tinto, Fonterra/Edendale, Ballance Agri-Nutrients, forestry exporters, MSC and other shipping lines) rather than consumer-facing
business_model.geographic_mix: Single-region: essentially 100% of operations are the Port of Bluff serving the Southland (and to a lesser extent Otago) catchment of New Zealand; end-market demand is split between NZ agriculture/industry (domestic) and export markets (China for logs, various markets for aluminium and dairy/meat)

main_competitors: Napier Port (for some coastal fertiliser/dairy freight)
Road/rail freight leakage to North Island ports
competitive_position.market_position: Natural monopoly for Southland's seaborne trade - South Port is the only deepwater commercial port in the region, giving it a structural catchment advantage, but it is a small player nationally and competes for marginal/contestable freight (particularly some fertiliser coastal shipping and container routing) against Port Otago to the north.
competitive_position.market_share: Effectively 100% share of Southland-origin seaborne cargo given no rival deepwater port in the catchment; company-disclosed figures are volume-based (3.96m tonnes, 62,000 TEU in FY26) rather than framed as a national market-share number.

moat_factors.description: Only deepwater commercial port serving Southland; high cost and inefficiency for shippers to truck freight to Port Otago or further afield for most bulk and Tiwai-linked cargo

The Tiwai smelter's raw material imports (alumina, petroleum coke, pitch) and aluminium exports are physically adjacent to South Port's Tiwai Wharf, making the port the natural logistics point for the smelter for as long as it operates - but this cuts both ways as a concentration risk (see Key Risks)
Ports require extensive resource consents (e.g., the multi-year channel deepening/dredging consent process) that make a competing deepwater facility in the region highly unlikely

The entrance channel and berth pockets have been dredged to allow drafts up to 10.3m at high water (interim step toward a 10.7m target), letting larger vessels call with better payloads - a durable efficiency/cost advantage for customers versus alternative ports, cited by management as already delivering productivity gains for shipping lines

moat_factors.factor: Council ownership as a stability/reputational anchor
moat_factors.description: Majority local-government ownership signals long-term commitment to regional infrastructure and can support access to capital, but also caps commercial flexibility (see risks)

weaknesses: Small scale nationally - a minor port relative to Tauranga, Auckland, Lyttelton, and even Port Otago, limiting bargaining power with global shipping lines
Structural cargo concentration in one industrial customer (NZAS) and one primary industry (agriculture) tied to a single regional economy
Limited diversification benefit from being landlocked to Southland - cannot easily capture growth outside the region
Council-majority ownership can constrain M&A, capital raising flexibility, and takeover premium realization for minority holders

growth_drivers: Recovery and stabilisation of NZAS/Tiwai smelter volumes following the 2025 Meridian Energy demand-response curtailment - third potline back to full operation as of H1 FY26

Renewable energy project cargo - Southland/Otago wind farm construction pipeline (Kaiwera Downs Stage 2, Puke Kapo Hau Stage 2 consented July 2026 at 190MW, Southland Wind Farm consented April 2026 at 325MW; ~1,851MW of projects across various stages of development in the region, expected to be built over a 5-10 year horizon) - a multi-year, though lumpy, tailwind for imported turbine components and marine/handling revenue

Bluff Freight Centre / warehousing expansion - purchase and upgrade of the Foreshore Road cold-storage facility (4,000m2 dry storage + 2,400m2 hardstand) to dairy-warehousing standard, supporting growing Fonterra Edendale export volumes, operational from Q3 CY2026

Container growth via new shipping services - MSC Eagle Service (direct US East Coast/Europe link via Panama, launched mid-Feb 2026) and enhanced Trans-Tasman Southern Loop, plus rising MSC Wallaby Service call frequency

Post-channel-deepening productivity - larger vessel calls and higher payloads per call already reducing shippers' per-call costs (25% of large vessel calls in H1 FY26 used the deeper draft at both tide states), which should support volume/vessel-size growth without proportional new capex

30-year Port Planning Exercise (with Gloco/Dennis Koegeboehn, first two stages due late September 2026) targeting landside productivity optimisation and identifying further growth ("transformation") capex options out to 2057
Emerging aquaculture and other large-scale regional development opportunities progressing through the fast-track consenting process
Coastal shipping potential - discussions with Ballance Agri-Nutrients on longer-term coastal fertiliser trade from its Awarua plant following the Mount Maunganui facility closure

business.description: NZAS/Tiwai Wharf volumes were ~24% of South Port's total FY26 trade tonnage (942,000 of 3.96m tonnes) and management explicitly attributes part of the FY26 revenue and profit recovery to smelter volumes normalising after a 50MW Meridian Energy demand-response curtailment event in February 2025 that had depressed FY25 volumes. A precise Tiwai share of REVENUE (as opposed to volume) is not disclosed by the company in the reviewed filings; one third-party estimate (an older, ~2021-era figure sourced from a search snippet, not verified against a primary filing) put Tiwai revenue as low as NZ$5.6m against total company revenue at the time, reflecting that some Tiwai cargo has historically generated little/no wharfage. This should be treated as directionally indicative only - the true current Tiwai revenue share is materially uncertain and could be higher given growth in fixed-fee elements. The 20-year NZAS electricity supply agreements signed May 2024 (Meridian, Contact, Mercury, ~572MW aggregate, running to at least 2044) substantially de-risk an outright smelter closure over the medium term, but embed demand-response provisions allowing NZAS to be asked to curtail up to a combined 185MW of consumption at times of national supply stress - directly the mechanism that caused the FY25 volume shortfall and remains a recurring risk to Tiwai-linked cargo in future dry/high-demand years.
business.quantification_basis: 24% of FY26 volume is company-disclosed (investor presentation, 21-Aug-2026); revenue share is NOT company-disclosed and is flagged here as an estimate gap

business.description: 100% of operations are tied to the Southland regional economy; a downturn in Southland agriculture, forestry, or industrial activity has no offsetting geographic diversification

NZ log exports to China have faced soft demand (China log imports down ~22% YoY Jan-Sep 2025 per trade press; CFR A-grade prices under periodic pressure), though prices showed some recovery through mid/late 2026; South Port's FY26 log volumes were flattered by a one-off wind-throw weather event rather than a clean demand recovery, per the FY26 presentation

business.risk: Loss of contestable freight to Port Otago/Lyttelton
business.description: Some fertiliser, container and general freight is contestable via road/rail to competing South Island ports; South Port's catchment monopoly is strong for Southland-origin bulk/Tiwai cargo but weaker at the margin for routed container traffic

Management explicitly flagged in the FY26 result (21-Aug-2026) that FY27 volumes are expected to be broadly flat versus FY26 due to the absence of one-off wind-farm project cargo that boosted FY26 (16,000+ tonnes of turbine components); this is a company-acknowledged near-term earnings headwind

financial.description: Company flags likely need for a replacement tug and mobile harbour crane in the short-to-medium term, plus potential further "transformation" capex flowing from the 30-year Port Planning Exercise (results due late Sept 2026); management commits to a minimum WACC return hurdle but scale/timing of this capex is not yet quantified

Gross debt flat at $31.0m FY25→FY26; net debt reduced to $18.5m (from $25m) with Debt/EBITDA of 0.6x (down from 1.0x) and $19.0m of covenant headroom - currently a low-risk balance sheet, but a large future capex cycle (as in FY21-24) would re-lever the company

financial.risk: High dividend payout ratio limits reinvestment buffer
financial.description: FY26 payout ratio was 47% of NPAT (29.0 cps declared, up from 28.0 cps FY25); as an income-oriented stock, a significant earnings shock (e.g., a Tiwai curtailment repeat) would pressure the dividend or require higher leverage to maintain it

regulatory.description: As a dredging, marine and industrial operator co-located with an aluminium smelter, South Port faces ongoing resource consent obligations (e.g., the multi-year channel deepening consent process) and environmental scrutiny, particularly given its council ownership and proximity to Foveaux Strait/Awarua Rūnaka interests

regulatory.risk: Majority council ownership constrains takeover/control premium
regulatory.description: Environment Southland's ~66% stake means no change-of-control transaction can occur without council/ratepayer support, effectively removing takeover-premium optionality for minority shareholders and tying governance outcomes to local-body political dynamics; no public indication was found in this research of an announced intention by Environment Southland to sell down its stake

NZAS is a large carbon-intensive industrial customer; future changes to NZ climate policy, carbon pricing, or global aluminium demand/decarbonisation trends could affect smelter operating levels and thus Tiwai-linked port volumes

macro.risk: NZ dollar and global freight/shipping conditions
macro.description: Red Sea shipping disruption continues to affect global vessel transit patterns (transits remained ~60% below pre-conflict levels per the H1 FY26 interim report), an indirect but real influence on shipping line routing, service frequency and cost through Bluff

Fonterra's farmgate milk price forecast was revised down to $8.50-$9.50/kgMS (from $8.00-$11.00) through late CY2025 per the H1 FY26 report; sustained weak dairy pricing could eventually reduce farm input import volumes and Edendale-linked export container volumes, though no reduction had yet been observed by the company as of Feb 2026
macro.watch: company committed to monitoring over the following six months

macro.risk: Hydro/electricity system stress driving further NZAS curtailment
macro.description: South Island hydro lake storage levels were healthy (113% of historic mean) as of Feb 2026, but the FY25 precedent shows that a dry/high-demand period can trigger a Meridian demand-response call on NZAS, directly hitting Tiwai wharf volumes and South Port revenue

Port throughput is tied to broader trade volumes, agricultural commodity cycles and industrial activity, all of which have some sensitivity to interest rates and global growth, though South Port's diversified cargo mix has historically dampened cyclicality (5-yr cargo tonnage CAGR of ~3.05%, revenue CAGR ~6.5%)

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ port sector is mature and consolidated around a handful of regional gateways; SPN's own cargo base grew at a ~3.05% 5-year volume CAGR and ~6.5% 5-year revenue CAGR, modestly ahead of typical GDP-linked port growth, aided by Southland's agricultural intensification and emerging renewable-energy project cargo
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate - diversified bulk/container/industrial mix cushions single-commodity cycles, but the concentrated regional economy and the binary nature of smelter demand-response events create lumpy year-to-year swings (illustrated by the FY25 dip and FY26 recovery)
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Low-moderate direct - modest net debt (0.6x EBITDA) and a long-term gearing target of <2.0x limit direct rate sensitivity; indirect sensitivity through customers' capex decisions (e.g., wind farm project timing) and consumer/dairy demand
macro_factors.currency_exposure: NZD-denominated revenue and costs; indirect exposure through export commodity pricing (logs priced in USD/China demand, aluminium priced in USD) affecting customer volumes

recent_developments.event: FY26 (year to 30 June 2026) record result announced: revenue $71.8-71.9m (+13.5-14%), EBITDA $29.9m (+15.7-16%), reported NPAT $16.11m (+21.0%), normalised NPAT $16.14m (+16.2%); full-year dividend declared at 29.0 cps fully imputed (FY25: 28.0 cps), 47% payout ratio; net debt fell to $18.5m from $25m, Debt/EBITDA 0.6x

recent_developments.date: 2026-08-2026 (~4 days before search, i.e. late Aug 2026)
recent_developments.event: Capital Change Notice / Employee Share Rights Plan - unquoted share rights issued for nil cash consideration (35,987 rights disclosed in one NZX filing), each converting 1:1 into ordinary shares; part of a broader employee share rights plan referenced in the task brief

CEO Derek Nind formally commenced/was confirmed effective July 2026 following Nigel Gear's departure after 8.5 years as CEO (30+ years total tenure); Chair Philip Cory-Wright to retire from the Board in October 2026 at the ASM, succeeded by Nicola Greer

"SPN Leadership Transition Update and Trading Commentary" NZX announcement - confirmed Gear's end-May 2026 departure, Derek Nind's appointment effective 27 July 2026 (Geoff Finnerty as interim CEO in between), and Cory-Wright's planned October 2026 Board retirement

H1 FY26 interim result announced: record half revenue $34.75m (+17.6%), EBITDA $15.29m (+23.4%), reported NPAT $8.45m (+46.8%), normalised NPAT $8.56m (+36.0%); interim dividend 8.5 cps (up from 7.5 cps) paid 10 March 2026; cargo volumes +17.8% to 1.99m tonnes, Tiwai volumes +30.0% to 0.51m tonnes as NZAS's third potline returned to full operation after the Feb-2025 demand-response curtailment

Appointment of two new independent directors, Peter Barker (ex-CFO Computershare, ex-VP Finance BHP) and Jacqui Nelson (ex-Chief Generation/Development Officer, Contact Energy), following director Michelle Henderson's departure from the Board (effective 27 Jan 2026) to become General Manager of NZAS at Tiwai Point - underscoring the close personnel/commercial ties between the port and its largest industrial customer

Purchase of the Foreshore Road cold-storage facility near Bluff Township (4,000m2, plus 2,400m2 hardstand), subsequently upgraded to dairy-warehousing standard (the "Bluff Freight Centre") to support growing Fonterra Edendale export volumes, operational from Q3 CY2026

Wind farm project cargo - two vessels carrying Kaiwera Downs Stage 2 turbine components arrived Oct 2025 with a further three scheduled for Q1 CY2026; Southland Wind Farm (325MW) consented April 2026 and Puke Kapo Hau Stage 2 (190MW) consented July 2026, adding to a regional pipeline of ~1,851MW of wind projects at various stages
MSC Eagle Service launched (direct NZ-to-US East Coast link via Panama with European connections), complementing the enhanced Trans-Tasman Southern Loop, supporting record container growth

items.vs_prior: no explicit prior FY27 guidance to compare (first FY27 guide); flagged as a step-down in growth momentum versus FY26's +11.5%
items.notes: Company explicitly flags downside risk from the absence of the one-off wind farm project cargo that boosted FY26, plus incremental resourcing and maintenance investment
Management stated current market conditions make it "challenging to provide a firm forecast for FY27"; a further update was promised at the Annual Shareholders' Meeting in October 2026

items.target: likely replacement of a tug and mobile harbour crane in the short-to-medium term; further capex pending Port Planning Exercise Stage 1/2 findings (due late Sept 2026) and potential Stage 3 "Transformation Options"
items.notes: All growth capex is subject to a minimum WACC return hurdle per stated capital management policy; company targets a 'shadow' investment-grade credit profile and a long-term gearing target of Net Debt/EBITDA <2.0x (currently 0.6x)

items.target: no explicit FY27 cents-per-share target disclosed
items.notes: Company reiterated a commitment to "sustainable shareholder returns balancing reinvestment needs with disciplined capital distribution"; FY26 final dividend of 29.0 cps represented a gross yield of ~4.8% (net ~3.5%) on the $8.36 share price at 30 June 2026

guidance.management_commentary: Incoming CEO Derek Nind highlighted that bulk cargo remains South Port's core trade with growth from agriculture, forestry and renewable-energy project cargo, alongside 'stable operations' at NZAS. Outgoing Chair Philip Cory-Wright emphasised disciplined investment, customer service, and prudent planning. The company is explicit that FY27 faces a step-down from FY26's project-cargo-boosted growth and flags geopolitical/global uncertainty as a swing factor.

kpi_definitions.cargo_tonnes: Total physical weight (metric tonnes) of cargo handled across all trade types (bulk, container, Tiwai Wharf) - the primary volume KPI; FY26 total was 3.96 million tonnes
kpi_definitions.TEU: Twenty-foot Equivalent Unit - standard container-counting measure; FY26 record was 62,000 TEU (equivalent to ~665,000 tonnes)
kpi_definitions.bulk_cargo: Non-containerised cargo handled in bulk form (e.g., fertiliser, cement, stock feed, alumina, woodchip, logs) via the Bluff Wharves - 59% of FY26 trade volume
kpi_definitions.breakbulk_project_cargo: Large, individually handled cargo such as wind-turbine components, distinct from standard bulk or container flows; contributed 16,000+ tonnes in FY26 from wind farm imports
kpi_definitions.Tiwai_Wharf_volumes: Cargo specific to the New Zealand Aluminium Smelter - raw material imports (alumina, petroleum coke, pitch) and finished aluminium exports handled via the dedicated Tiwai Wharf; 24% of FY26 trade volume
kpi_definitions.vessel_calls: Number of large vessel visits to the port, a proxy for shipping line service frequency and scheduling; H1 FY26 large vessel calls were 154, up 17.5%
kpi_definitions.OFCF: Operating Free Cash Flow - net cash flow from operations less maintenance capex, plus cash from asset sales; FY26 OFCF was $18.4m
kpi_definitions.EBITDA_margin: EBITDA as a percentage of operating revenue; FY26 was ~41.6-42%, above the disclosed NZ port-sector average of ~38% (FY25) but below SPN's own 10-year high of ~44%

bull_case: Structural regional monopoly - South Port is the only deepwater commercial port serving Southland, giving it durable pricing power and no realistic risk of a competing local facility being built

Multi-year visibility on its largest customer risk - the 20-year NZAS electricity agreements (to at least 2044) materially reduce the probability of an outright Tiwai smelter closure that dominated the investment case a few years ago, and FY26 already shows volumes recovering from the FY25 demand-response dip

Diversified, growing cargo base beyond Tiwai - record bulk (agriculture-driven) and record container volumes in FY26, plus a multi-year regional wind-farm construction pipeline (~1,851MW of projects in development) providing a new, durable source of project cargo over 5-10 years

Strong balance sheet and disciplined capital allocation - net debt/EBITDA of just 0.6x, $19m of covenant headroom, a WACC-return hurdle on growth capex, and a high (47% FY26), fully imputed, consistently growing dividend makes this an attractive income holding for NZ investors

Recently completed channel deepening is already delivering measurable, low-incremental-cost productivity gains for customers (larger vessels, better payloads), a durable competitive edge without requiring further major capex to monetise
bear_case: Tiwai/NZAS concentration remains the single largest identifiable risk - ~24% of FY26 volume is smelter-linked, and the 2025 demand-response curtailment (up to 185MW available under the current power agreements) is a proven, recurring mechanism that can cut Tiwai cargo and profit with little warning in dry hydro years; the exact revenue (not just volume) exposure is not clearly disclosed by the company, which itself is a transparency risk for investors

FY27 is explicitly guided to be flat-to-down versus FY26 due to the loss of one-off wind farm project cargo, with management declining to give firm quantitative guidance - a rare acknowledgement of near-term earnings uncertainty right after a record year

Environment Southland's ~66% ownership caps takeover optionality and keeps the free float very small and illiquid, meaning minority shareholders are unlikely to ever see a control premium and the stock can trade on thin volumes with wide spreads

Single-region economic dependency - a Southland-specific downturn (dairy price weakness, forestry/log market softness driven by China demand, or reduced agricultural investment) has no geographic diversification to offset it

Leadership and Board transition risk - FY26 saw the retirement of a CEO with 30+ years' tenure (8.5 as CEO), the departure of a director to NZAS itself, two new independent directors, and an incoming Chair, all within about a year; execution risk during this transition period is elevated even though the company frames it as orderly
